answers.label: Benefits and challenges of consequential methods
answers.text:
The potential benefits of robust consequential accounting methods for electricity sector actions are significant, including providing recognition and incentives for more impactful or cost-effective GHG mitigation actions inside and outside of organizations’ Scope 2 footprints. But there are significant risks associated with their use, and it is likely that a poorly implemented approach would do more harm than good. These risks stem primarily from the fact that the results of consequential accounting are by definition unverifiable, being assessments of the difference in outcomes between unobservable counterfactual realities. This means that consequential assessments will always be subject to deep uncertainty, and the best we can do is to craft methodologies that appear as theoretically robust as possible.

At the same time, corporations can be expected to utilize consequential accounting to identify and pursue actions that enable the largest GHG mitigation claims at the least cost. While this is often presented as a benefit, it also makes the challenge of ‘baseline setting’ in consequential accounting more difficult. Because the lowest-cost mitigation efforts are also the least likely to have needed additional financial support, there is a thin line between a system that accurately incentivizes the most cost-effective actions, and one that incorrectly rewards non-impactful actions. The challenge in determining whether interventions are additional and impactful compared to a baseline is one that has plagued the carbon offset market (which is also based on consequential accounting and has attempted to implement methods similar to those proposed here in the electricity sector), leading to a collapse in public trust in offset impact claims.

Developing sufficiently robust consequential accounting methods is a worthy goal, but many challenges must be overcome. Above all, electricity sector consequential accounting must be sufficiently credible and conservative in its handling of baseline setting, additionality, and market leakage, to minimize the likelihood that it becomes a vehicle for greenwashing. The chosen system should also be flexible and detailed enough to retain accuracy across the diverse global tapestry of electricity system regulatory and market structures, while at the same time remaining standardized enough to be practically usable and comparable across organizations.

GHGP must also ensure that GHG impact claims resulting from electricity sector consequential accounting practices are made with appropriate acknowledgement of the uncertainties involved. Consequential claims should be clearly presented as estimates rather than measurements, and should be kept separate in public communication from the fundamentally verifiable measurements that underpin attributional Scope 2 accounting. A balanced approach that acknowledges the advantages and shortcomings of both consequential accounting and Scope 2 inventory accounting will be most effective at driving real impact and maintaining public trust over the long run.

Finally, we recommend that GHGP consider the incentives created by the promotion of consequential accounting alongside traditional inventory accounting. Proposed revisions to GHGP’s Scope 2 inventory guidance, which CATF supports, may make it more difficult for organizations to report zero inventory emissions. If a consequential accounting approach is developed that is not robust, and makes it easy for organizations to claim net-zero emissions impact, companies may de-emphasize inventory reporting and elevate better-looking consequential reporting in its place. We therefore recommend that GHGP require reporting of inventory results alongside any consequential reporting, to give the public an accurate picture of the extent to which companies are both decarbonizing their own operations and driving global impact. This ensures that both goals remain at the forefront of corporate sustainability efforts.

answers.label: Secondary effects to consider, and how
answers.text:
Secondary effects should at the very least include impacts on the deployment, retirement, and operation of other electricity sector assets. These would ideally be quantified by estimating the expected behaviors of these other assets in a ‘status quo’ world where the intervention did not take place and comparing those estimates to observed outcomes.

While it would also be technically accurate to include a host of other secondary impacts (e.g. economic, political, technology development) these are likely too abstract to quantify with any degree of confidence.

answers.label: Why annual or lifetime reporting
answers.text: Impact estimates are likely to change substantially as new information becomes available over the lifetime of a project and new operational decisions are made. While reported impacts will always be uncertain, they should not be based on information that is potentially decades out of date.

answers.label: Requiredness of the financial analysis test
Requiredness of the common practice test
Why selected tests should be included
answers.text:
Regulatory and timing tests should be required because they are easy to implement and are obvious disqualifiers if failed. Projects that were already mandated or in progress prior to a buyer’s participation should not be considered additional.

A common practice test should be required because it is feasible to implement and addresses perhaps the greatest challenge in consequential accounting – ensuring that actions which are already widely economical are not credited with outsize impact.

A contractual/tenor test should be required because long-term contracts are well understood to be key enablers of project finance. While spot market purchases of instruments like EACs can theoretically incentivize growth in clean generation, the connection is much more tenuous and disputed compared to direct long-term offtake.

answers.label: Context on test feasibility
answers.text:
Tests that define clear, objective thresholds and rely on information that is widely publicly available are generally feasible.

A financial analysis test is likely not feasible because it requires disclosure of sensitive financial information and relies on standards that are not easily provable (i.e. that a project’s value to any other buyer would be lower than a certain threshold).

Both the barrier test and performance standard test are fairly complex and subjective, and would be very difficult to implement in a credible manner.

answers.label: Regions warranting different tests, with examples
answers.text: Regional factors will almost certainly play a role in the validity of certain additionality tests. For example, some regions may have carbon cap regulations that make it difficult for any individual intervention to drive impact, while others may have forms of top-down planning or programs to incentivize private sector clean energy procurement. At the same time, it is important that whatever system is adopted be as globally consistent as possible, so that bespoke practices that harm comparability do not need to be developed for each region. Ideally, there will be a clear set of global guidelines determining which tests are applicable under which sets of policy or market conditions.

answers.label: Claims possible under different test approaches
answers.text: If an organization merely procures clean power that is provably non-additional, they should be able to advertise this procurement but not claim any emissions impact. Any claims of impact should be contingent on high confidence in the additionality of the intervention in question, and even then should be presented as estimates.

answers.label: Details on operating margin methodologies
answers.text:
Options (a) through (c) are generally appropriate methodologies because they are based on the same essential SCED logic that governs the operation of real grids. They should in theory produce relatively consistent results, though this assumption would ideally be tested before any set of methodologies is officially adopted. The remaining methodologies rely on various sets of assumptions that are more tenuously connected to the actual practice of grid operation.

One glaring gap in these methodologies as presented is the absence of any clear solution to quantifying the marginal emissions associated with discharge from energy storage, which is increasingly becoming a short-run marginal resource in grids worldwide. Even if storage can successfully be identified as a marginal generator (and this will be difficult under some methodologies given that storage bids based on opportunity cost rather than a predictable variable cost of operation), it is very difficult to calculate the emissions rate that should be assigned to that storage discharge. Appropriately tracking marginal emission rates during hours when storage is charging and assigning those emissions to discharge, while assessing the uncertainty involved, will be essential for the success of any operating margin methodology.

answers.label: Details on build margin methodologies
answers.text:
A build margin methodology that tracks recent capacity additions may be the only appropriate option, because it is based on empirical evidence. It is not a perfect approach, since the build margin implied by recent additions likely lags the instantaneous build margin if the pace of additions is changing rapidly, but it reflects a reasonable view of the resources whose deployment decisions might be affected by the intervention being assessed. In addition to capacity additions, this metric should also aim to take into account the impacts of avoided or accelerated capacity retirements.

The other proposed methodologies are generally unsuitable. The policy scenario option is based on national pledges rather than evidence of actual outcomes. Capacity expansion modeling is a useful tool for assessing potential future electricity system outcomes or comparing counterfactual scenarios, but it cannot predict actual system outcomes with high accuracy. An average emission rate approach is inappropriate because this metric has no relationship with either short- or long-run marginal emission rates.

Finally, if a build margin methodology based on recent additions is adopted, it must reflect the shape of the intervention being assessed in relation to the shape of the generation types on the build margin. For example, if the intervention is a new solar farm, its build margin impacts should be based on recently-built resources that generated at the same time as the solar farm’s expected generation (likely other solar farms). If this is not the case, interventions would be credited for displacing resources with which they do not directly compete.

answers.label: Assessing model applicability to project types
answers.text: There should be a single universal methodology for assessing the impacts of all projects. A usable, comparable methodology should allow as little user choice and subjectivity as possible, and should not incentivize pursuit of certain classes of projects due to their accounting advantages. Factors such as production shape are relevant to all generator types.

answers.label: Why that spatial granularity ceiling
answers.text: Any consequential method should adopt a level of spatial and temporal granularity that is at least equivalent to that of the proposed Scope 2 market-based method revisions.

answers.label: Why that temporal granularity ceiling
answers.text: Any consequential method should adopt a level of spatial and temporal granularity that is at least equivalent to that of the proposed Scope 2 market-based method revisions. Given the central role that variable renewables are likely to play in impact claims, time of generation and the resources with which an intervention competes are particularly critical factors to capture. A simple example illustrates the importance of hourly resolution: a grid where midday electricity demand is increasingly or entirely supplied by solar power, while demand at night is supplied by fossil power. If build and operating marginal emissions rates (and therefore impacts) are calculated at daily or higher resolution, it will appear that new solar power has a significant impact on emissions since the grid in question is still largely fossil-powered. Hourly resolution would reveal that new solar power largely displaces other solar on the build (and possibly operating) margin, and therefore has much less impact on emissions. This visibility is necessary to ensure that participants target times and locations where their interventions are most likely to be impactful.

answers.label: Why selected weighting approaches are appropriate
answers.text: Of the options listed here, an intervention lifecycle approach is likely the most appropriate. This option recognizes that in most cases, build margin impacts are likely to dominate over the long run as a project’s existence is factored into investment decisions in similar projects. The option is not without its flaws though, as it may not adequately capture the impacts of projects that adjust their operational approach on an ongoing basis (e.g. storage and demand-side management). More work will be needed, ideally in the form of both empirical investigation and energy system modeling, to assess the accuracy of this option.

answers.label: Weighting approaches not feasible to implement
Other approaches for assigning margin weights
answers.text: It may be reasonable to assign weights differently depending on whether an intervention is primarily operational (e.g. demand shifting or storage operations) or capacity-based (e.g. installation of a solar or wind farm that will operate predictably over its life). Capacity-based interventions should trend toward 100% build margin weighting, while it may make sense to maintain a higher operating margin weighting for operational interventions.

answers.label: Research supporting the suggested approach
answers.text: There is a dire lack of supporting evidence for any of the potential approaches listed here. Without some form of validation (e.g. analysis of a methodology’s accuracy in the controlled setting of an electricity system capacity expansion model as in https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=5985015, or case studies showing what projects deployed in different contexts would report), the chosen approach cannot be considered scientifically accurate or credible. This is of critical importance because an inaccurate weighting, e.g. giving operating margin a 50% weighting in a context where it should be 0%, could allow a completely non-impactful project to receive significant credit. This would directly incentivize the same behaviors that have plagued voluntary carbon markets in recent years, and would open GHGP to accusations of enabling greenwashing. The working groups responsible for developing any consequential metrics should consider building an affirmative evidence base to be a critical part of their work.
